INTRODUCTION
Ramos resolves this case.  It sets the stakes:  The
Sixth Amendment’s “promise of  a jury trial” is “fundamental to the American scheme of justice.”  Ramos v.
Louisiana, 590 U.S. 83, 89, 93 (2020).  It sets the test:
The scope of that right is controlled by “what the term
‘trial by an impartial jury’ meant at the time of the Sixth
Amendment’s adoption.”  Id. at 90.  And it determines
the outcome:  “[C]ommon law, state practices in the
founding era [and] opinions and treatises written soon
afterward,” id., establish that the Sixth Amendment
guarantees the right to a 12-person jury.
Florida cannot seriously dispute that “a mountain of
evidence suggests that, both at the time of the Amendment’s adoption and for most of our Nation’s history, the
right to a trial by jury for serious criminal offenses
meant a trial before 12 members of the community[.]”
Khorrami v. Arizona, 143 S.Ct. 22, 23 (2022) (Gorsuch,
J., dissenting from denial of certiorari).  To the contrary,
Florida repeatedly acknowledges “history shows that
the default common-law jury size was 12 in 1791.”
Fla.Br.1; see also Fla.Br.9, 11.
To escape the historical record and Ramos, Florida
relies on constitutional tests announced in two other
cases—Dobbs and Williams itself.  Fla.Br.6-9.  According to Florida, these decisions mean that the Constitution’s failure to use the number “12” requires Mr. Kian
to prove a particular number of jurors was “so essential
… as to be impliedly codified[.]”  Fla.Br.9.  But Ramos
expressly rejects “distinguish[ing] between the historic
features of common law jury trials that (we think) serve
‘important enough’ functions to migrate silently into the
Sixth Amendment and those that don’t.”  590 U.S. at 98.

2


Regardless, Dobbs focused on the rule for whether an
unenumerated right should be read into the Due Process
Clause—not interpreting the scope of the Sixth Amendment.  And Williams, for its part, expressly disavowed
reliance on “purely historical considerations” in favor of
a functionalist approach.  Williams v. Florida, 399 U.S.
78, 89, 99 (1970).
Unable to prevail on the hi story or the law, Florida
falls back on threats, asserting that enforcing the original public meaning of the Sixth Amendment will be the
end of Miranda warnings, court-appointed criminal defense attorneys, and “[m]odern Eighth Amendment jurisprudence” itself.  Fla.B r.2, 45-49, 51.  But if that Rubicon were real, Ramos crossed it—the dissenting Justices suggested that decisions like Miranda, Gideon, and
Furman were “all now up for grabs[.]”  Ramos, 590 U.S.
at 153 (Alito, J., dissenting).  Thankfully, Florida is
wrong.  Apodaca and Williams are uniquely and closely
linked.  Pet.Br.26-28.  As Ramos ’s detractors observed
seven years ago, the Court could not have ruled in favor
of Mr. Ramos without implicitly “overturn[ing] Williams.”  Ramos Louisiana Br.19, No. 18-5924; see also
Ramos Oregon Br.27 (“[O]ne could mount a challenge to
Williams by taking much of the briefing in [Ramos] and
substituting … ‘the rule of 12’ for unanimity.”); Ramos,
590 U.S. at 158 (Alito, J., dissenting) (“[r]epudiating the
reasoning of Apodaca will almost certainly prompt calls
to overrule Williams”).
Nor will recognizing the right to a 12-person jury
force a change in criminal procedure outside of Florida
and the other six States that permit small juries to hear
felonies that could result in a significant term of imprisonment.  Cf. Fla.Br.2.  Mr. Kian was convicted of five felony counts of practicing chir opractic medicine with a

3


suspended license and faced decades in prison.
Pet.Br.14.1  The only question this Court need address is
whether the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments protect
his right to a 12-person jury  in light of being charged
with those serious felonies.  This Court accordingly need
not resolve, for example, whether certain misdemeanors
require 12 jurors, Fla.Br.36, or the constitutionality of
Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 23(b)(3), U.S.Br.29-
32.  Such questions should be answered, if at all, on another day.  See, e.g., Fuld v. Palestine Liberation Org. ,
606 U.S. 1, 18-19 (2025) (reserving judgment on “the
Fifth Amendment’s outer limits” because “the cases before us do not require doing so”).
To be sure, applying Ramos’s reasoning to the 12-
person jury requirement will require some cases currently on direct appeal to be retried.  Adopting “new
rules of criminal procedure usually” does, with such decisions “often affecting si gnificant numbers of pending
cases across the whole country.”  Ramos, 590 U.S. at 108.
But the seven States’ “competing interests” cannot outweigh “the reliance the American people place in their
constitutionally protected liberties[.]”  Id. at 111 (plurality op.).

1 Florida’s gratuitous assertions of sexual misconduct (Fla.Br.i,
3, 51) were not the basis for Mr. Kian’s convictions or even properly
before the jury, see Trial Tr. 191 (Oct. 30, 2023) (court instructing
prosecution not to “get into” such allegations, as Mr. Kian “is not
charged with any kind of Battery, SV, anything like that”).

4


ARGUMENT
I. THE CONSTITUTION GUARANTEED MR. KIAN A
12-PERSON JURY
A. Florida Relies On The Wrong Historical Test
As explained, Ramos requires courts to determine
the “meaning” of “trial by an impartial jury” by considering the public understanding of the term at the time of
the Sixth Amendment’s adoption.  Pet.Br.16-17.  That inquiry requires consulting “the common law, state practices in the founding era, [and]  opinions and treatises
written soon afterward.”  Pet.Br.17.  Ramos thus rejects
the Williams approach of “distinguish[ing] between the
historic features of common law jury trials that (we
think) serve ‘important enough’ functions to migrate silently into the Sixth Amendmen t and those that don’t.”
590 U.S. at 98.
Florida’s view of how to interpret the Sixth Amendment cannot be reconciled with Ramos’s.
Florida first places weight on the fact that “the Constitution’s text ‘makes no express reference’ to a particular right” to 12-person juries.  Fla.Br.6 (quoting Dobbs
v. Jackson Women’s Health Org., 597 U.S. 215, 235
(2022)).  Even setting aside that Dobbs focused on the
scope of the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process
Clause, the Sixth Amendment makes no reference to
unanimity either.  But as Ramos explained, the Constitution does expressly protect the right to a jury trial.
590 U.S. at 89.  That right must be given meaning.  And
the way to do so is to consider what “the right to a jury
trial meant” to the public “at the time of the [Sixth]
Amendment’s adoption.”  Id. at 98.  Florida’s approach
would leave a “right mentioned twice in the Constitution
… an empty promise.”  Id.

5


Florida next asserts that the Court must consider
what the Framers “ believed indispensable” to—or
“meant to incorporate” in—the right to a jury trial.  E.g.,
Fla.Br.7, 18 n.5, 38 (emphases added).  This is just another restatement of the Apodaca test, which sought in
the first instance to divine “the intent of the Framers.”
Apodaca v. Oregon, 406 U.S. 404, 410 (1972) (citing Williams as the origin for this test).  In overruling Apodaca,
Ramos rejected this line of thinking.  The original public
meaning of “the language Congress retained and the
States ratified” provides the bounds of the Sixth
Amendment, regardless of “why” that language was
chosen.  590 U.S. at 98.
Florida then appears to suggest that Mr. Kian must
prove every American trial from the Founding to Reconstruction used a 12-person jury.  Fla.Br.9-21.  Much of
Florida’s supposed evidence of variations in criminal
jury size is wrong.  See infra pp.7-12.  Regardless, Ramos did not hold the original public meaning of the jury
trial right to Florida’s standard.  Instead, the Court recognized that a degree of historical “variation[] did not
matter much.”  Ramos, 590 U.S. at 90.  And Ramos observed that “a few of the Colonies,” including the Carolinas, “had relaxed … the unanimity requirement” and
“permitted conviction by majority vote.”  Id. at 91 n.15;
see also Ramos Louisiana Br.16-17 (arguing “Foundingera practice contradicts the notion that the Framers expected the words ‘trial by jury’ … to automatically trigger a unanimity requirement”).  At best, Florida can
identify the same kinds of  pre-founding variations, or
abridgements of the jury trial right that occurred nearly
a century after ratification of the Sixth Amendment.
Fla.Br.10-21; infra pp.7-12.

6


Finally, Florida asserts that because the commonlaw 12-person requirement could be modified by Parliament, the right incorporated within the Sixth Amendment must permit legislatures to reduce jury size.
Fla.Br.9-10, 13.  This argument confuses a general limitation on common-law rules with a specific limitation on
the 12-person jury right.  In England, “the omnipotence
of parliament over the common law was absolute, even
against common right and reason.”  Hurtado v. California, 110 U.S. 516, 531 (1884).  “In this country,” however,
“written constitutions were deemed essential to protect
the rights and liberties of the people against the encroachments of power delegated to their governments[.]”  Id.  The jury trial is one of those rights and
liberties and cannot be “freely abridged by statute.”  Ramos, 590 U.S. at 89.  Were it otherwise, the Seventh
Amendment—which has a scope set by “common law”
principles—could be negated by Congress.  That cannot
be right.
B. Florida Cannot Prevail Under The Correct
Historical Test
As explained, the historical evidence is what matters, and it is unequivocal.  Pet.Br.5-11, 16-23.  Florida
itself agrees “the default jury size at common law was
12,” Fla.Br.9; 12 has been “the default” since around the
fourteenth century, Fla.Br.11; and a number of founding-era state courts read their jury guarantees “to implicitly require 12-person ju ries,” Fla.Br.15 n.3.  Under
Ramos, that means the Sixth Amendment required Mr.
Kian to be tried before 12 jurors.  Florida identifies nothing undermining that conclusion.

7


1. Pre-Founding Sources
Many of Florida’s supposed examples do not involve
criminal juries at all.  Florida opens with Norman and
Frankish proceedings that “show all sorts of numbers.”
Fla.Br.10.  But by Florida’s own description, these bodies “gathered information for fiscal and administrative
purposes,” id.—i.e., they were not criminal trials.  Other
examples are similarly inapposite.  Florida admits that
Glanvill’s “jury of eight” was convened “to determine
the defense of infancy in land disputes,” id., not to try
crimes.  And Duncomb’s observation that “less than
Twelve may serve” in “Inquests of Office,” on “Writs to
inquire of Damages,” and for “‘Writs of Inquiry’ courts
[that] would award damages” again did not involve criminal proceedings.  Fla.Br.12; 3 Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England  258 (1768).  When he addressed criminal juries immediately before the passage
Florida quotes, he stated the rule clearly: “the Law is so
precise in this Number of Twelve, that if the Trial be by
more or less, it is a Mistrial.”  1 Duncomb, Trials per
Pais 92-93 (8th ed. 1766).2
Florida’s other purported examples of smaller juries
during this early period are also unavailing.  For example, Florida wrongly suggests (Fla.Br.13) that Blackstone equivocated on the size of a criminal jury, despite
his express statement that no one could be convicted of
a serious crime except by “the unanimous [s]uffrage of
twelve of his equals and neighbours.”  4 Blackstone, at
343.  Florida’s assertion (Fla.Br.13) that “elsewhere

2 The “juries of 9, 36, and 40” Thayer attributes to Bracton’s
Note Book also say little about legal re quirements for juries in the
13th century, as those numbers were at least “partly” attributable
to litigants’ “consent.”  Thayer, The Jury and Its Development, 5
Harv. L. Rev. 295, 295 (1892).

8


Blackstone treated the number as less material,” when
he mentioned only “a competent number of sensible and
upright jurymen,” omits the rest of the passage.  Blackstone states in the same breath that disputed facts “must
be examined and decided by twelve indifferent men.”
3 Blackstone, at 380 (emphasis added); see also id. at 379
(“unanimous consent of twelve”) (emphasis added).  Florida also invokes Tredymmock v. Perryman to suggest
juries of fewer than 12 were permissible at common law,
but later admits it is relying on an unsuccessful
“argu[ment]” not accepted by the court.  Compare
Fla.Br.11-12 with Tredymmock v. Perryman, 3 Croke,
Reports (7 Car. I) 259-260 (Thomas Leach 4th ed. 1793)
(conviction by six-person jury “void, and against the
common law”).
Finally, Florida suggests the “Duke’s Laws of
1665”—which it states were briefly adopted by a few
New York cities and two early colonies—deserve “special weight.”  Fla.Br.14.  But Ramos dismissed similar
colony-level experiments as not reflective of original
public meaning, given that “by the time of the Sixth
Amendment’s adoption, unanimity had again become the
accepted rule.”  590 U.S. at 91 n.15.  The same is true of
the Duke’s Laws.  Even by Florida’s account, for example, the newly founded colony of Pennsylvania operated
under the Duke’s Laws only “until 1683,” Fla.Br.15, and
the very source Williams (and Florida’s own brief in opposition) relied on in discussing Pennsylvania practice
described such proceedings as  “informal,” Pet.Br.7 n.3.
Pennsylvania’s laws subsequently guaranteed trials “by
twelve men, and, as near as may be, peers, or equals.”
Emerick v. Harris, 1 Binn. 416, 426 (Pa. 1808) (Brackenridge, J., op.); see also Prof.Su.Br.3-7.

9


2. Founding-Era Sources
Florida’s founding-era evidence begins with the observation that “[o]f the 13 state constitutions existing in
1791, only two specified that ju ries should consist of 12
members,” while the other 11 “said nothing of jury size.”
Fla.Br.15.  Again, Ramos rejected this same type of argument with respect to unanimity.  Not all founding-era
constitutions “explicitly required unanimity”—others
“preserved the right to a jury trial in more general
terms.”  590 U.S. at 90-91.  But the Court recognized “the
variations did not matter much; consistent with the common law, state courts appeared to regard unanimity as
an essential feature of the jury trial.”  Id.
The same logic applies here.  Pet.Br.19-20.  Even beyond the numerous States with laws or constitutions expressly requiring 12 members, others guaranteed “trial
by jury” in the common-law sense, and the state courts
that construed that term held that it meant 12.  See
Pet.Br.7, 9.  Tellingly, Florida identifies no founding-era
court that held otherwise.  Fla.Br.15 n.3.
Florida’s reliance on individual Framers is no more
persuasive.  For example, Florida leans heavily on
James Wilson’s remarks regarding “ civil juries” but ultimately concedes Wilson’s statements about criminal
juries “assumed the default 12-person jury.”  Fla.Br.15-
16 & n.4 (emphasis added); see Prof.Su.Br.16-18.  And to
the extent Florida relies on Wilson’s personal “predilection” about jury size, Fla.Br .15, such subjective considerations are constitutionally irrelevant, see supra p.5.
Other Framers Florida cites were not discussing
criminal jury size or the Sixth Amendment at all.  Mason
and Gorham were, as Florida acknowledges, “[s]peaking
of civil juries” in debating whether the Constitution

10


should include a civil jury clause.  Fla.Br.17 (citing 2 Records of the Federal Convention of 1787, pp.587, 628 (Max
Farrand ed., 1911) (“ Farrand’s Records”)).  Florida itself observes (Fla.Br.17) that Washington’s letter to
Lafayette concerned Article III, 3 Farrand’s Records
pp.288-298 (letter dated Apr. 28, 1788), and the “future
adjustment” to the Constitution that Washington references was ultimately made by ratifying the Bill of
Rights.  Madison’s remark at the Virginia convention
again said nothing of jury si ze and appears to have focused on the “vicinage” requirement later adapted by
the Sixth Amendment.  Id. pp.331-332 (remarks of June
20, 1788).  The Framers who did address the permissible
number of jurors said 12.  Pet.Br.8; see Constitutional.Ctr.Br.9-10; Prof.Su.Br.14-16; USCCB.Br.17-18.
Again, Florida identifies zero examples of Framers actually stating fewer than 12 jurors sufficed.  Cf.
Fla.Br.18 n.5.
Florida’s founding-era dictionaries follow the same
pattern.  Fla.Br.18-19.  Florida largely discusses dictionaries that do not address jury size at all.  It does not identify a single example of a dictionary stating that fewer
than 12 persons could constitute a jury.  And it omits
several that defined a jury as including 12 members.  See
Prof.Su.Br.11-12; USCCB.Br.9-11.  In fact, criminal juries were so associated with the number twelve that
“twelve men” (or similar variations) were frequently
used as a synonym for jury in 17th-19th century
“books, poems, devotionals, and trial pamphlets.”
USCCB.Br.11-12.
3. Early American Sources
Florida largely ignores American practice between
the founding and antebellum periods.  See Fla.Br.19-20.
For good reason: until at least the 1850s, scholars and

11


state courts consistently described the right to a trial by
jury as requiring 12 people.  Pet.Br.19-21.
Florida instead skips ahead to the Civil War era, arguing that five state constitutions enacted between 1850
and 1868—and four more adopted in former slave States
immediately after Reconstruction ended—permitted juries of fewer than 12 for ce rtain trials.  Fla.Br.19-20.
These examples cannot unwind the relevant historical
record—i.e., “what the term ‘trial by an impartial jury’
meant at the time of the Sixth Amendment’s adoption.”
Ramos, 590 U.S. at 90 (emphasis added).  Regardless,
Florida severely overstates its evidence.
Consider Florida’s very fi rst citation: Michigan.
Fla.Br.19.  Article VI, §28 of Michigan’s 1850 constitution states: “In every criminal prosecution, the accused
shall have the right to a speedy and public trial by an
impartial jury, which may consist of less than twelve
men in all courts not of record.”  People v. Antkoviak,
619 N.W.2d 18, 31 (Mich. Ct. App. 2000) (emphasis
added).  Florida never addresses the “not of record” proviso, which referred to courts that “adjudicated relatively minor offenses like misdemeanors.”  Id. at 36.
Michigan’s 1850 constitution therefore confirms Mr.
Kian’s position—felonies at least required 12 jurors.
Florida’s other examples have similar faults.  Florida cites Georgia’s 1868 constitution, eliding its earlier
admission that Georgia’s 1777 constitution expressly required 12 jurors.  Fla.Br.15, 19-20.  Prior to 1868, moreover, Georgia courts had consistently held that criminal
juries must consist of 12 people.  See, e.g., Boon v. State,
1 Ga. 618, 619 (1846) (noting constitution required a verdict by “twelve men”).  And even after the 1868 constitution, Georgia courts questioned whether juries
smaller than 12 were permitted “in cases of felony.”

12


Allen v. State , 51 Ga. 264, 266 (1874) (1868 constitution
permitted smaller juries for “trials for misdemeanors in
the county courts and other inferior tribunals established by law”).  Iowa’s 1857 constitution similarly restricted smaller juries to a subset of courts, and its supreme court has recognized the provision Florida cites
was “an express variance from what were then thought
to be the … essentials of a jury trial.”  Pitcher v. Lakes
Amusement Co., 236 N.W.2d 333, 337 (Iowa 1975).  Iowa
thus again confirms 12-person juries were considered
“essential[].”  Id.
Finally, Florida’s reference (Fla.Br.19) to South
Carolina’s 1865 constitution undermines its later assertion (Fla.Br.50-51) that small juries were implemented
for race-neutral reasons.  The provision Florida cites allowed smaller juries “wherein the accused is a person of
color.”  S.C. Const. art.III, §1 (1865); 1866 S.C. Sess.
Laws 493, §3. 3  This post-Civil War rule followed a tradition of permitting smaller panels to try enslaved people.  Juror Project Br.19.  For white defendants, “the
words ‘trial by jury’ in the South Carolina Constitution
meant ‘trial by twelve good and lawful men of the vicinage,’ and trial by fewer than twelve was ‘not a trial by
jury, in any sense in which the words have ever been legally used.’”  Id. (quoting State v. Simons , 29 S.C.L. (2
Speers) 761, 768 (S.C. Ct. Err. 1844)).

3 Florida cites S.C. Const. art.IX, §7 (1865).  That provision
states “the General Assembly sh all have power to determine the
number of persons who shall constitute the jury in the Inferior and
District Courts.”  S.C. Const. art. III, §1, in turn, states that “[t]he
General Assembly shall, as soon as possible, establish for each District in the State an Inferior Court or Courts, to be styled ‘The District Court,’” that “shall have ju risdiction” over civil and criminal
cases involving “a person of color.”

13


C. Requiring 12 Jurors Does Not Mean Other
Historical Features Of The Jury Must Be
Applied Today
Florida is wrong (Fla.Br.24-31) that if the Sixth
Amendment requires 12 jurors, it must constitutionalize
every other “accustomed requisite” of the 1791 jury.  See
Pet.Br.28, 35-36.  Ramos  rejected this same “parade of
horribles.”  590 U.S. at 100 n.47; id. at 154 & n.26 (Alito,
J., dissenting) (listing the exclusion of women, nonrandom selection of jurors, and trial judge commentary on
the facts as “aspects of late 18th-century jury practice”
encompassed by the majority’s rule).  Florida, moreover,
does not show that the other practices it highlights have
the same historical pedigree as unanimity or the 12-person requirement.  Fla.Br.24-31.  Juror qualifications, for
example, “varied considerably at common law[.]”  Ramos, 590 U.S. at 100 n.47.
 Florida also ignores that the Sixth Amendment
must be interpreted consistently with other constitutional guarantees.  Many of the features Florida speculates were historically common would run headlong into
such provisions, especially when harmful to jurors and
defendants.  For example, limiting juries “to middleclass propertied men,” Fla.Br.26 (emphasis omitted),
would violate “further constitutional amendments that
prohibit invidious discrimination.”  Ramos, 590 U.S. at
100 n.47.  A verdict from a jury deprived of food and water runs afoul of a defendant’s right to an “uncoerced
verdict.”  Lowenfield v. Phelps, 484 U.S. 231, 241 (1988).
And limited voir dire may contravene a defendant’s due
process right to have jurors questioned on potential bias.
See, e.g., Ham v. South Carolina, 409 U.S. 524, 527
(1973).  In any event, none of these questions are presented by this case, which involves an aspect of jury

14


practice closely linked to—and grounded in the same history as—the right in Ramos.  See supra pp.2, 4-5.
II. FLORIDA REWRITES WILLIAMS BUT CANNOT SAVE IT
Because Ramos abrogated Williams, this Court
need not perform a full-fledged stare decisis analysis.
Regardless, stare decisis poses no barrier to protecting
Mr. Kian’s right to a 12-person jury.
A. Florida Misstates The Stare Decisis Standard
Florida (Fla.Br.33) starts with the wrong law by relying on Kimble v. Marvel Entertainment, 576 U.S. 446
(2015).  That was a civil case where “ stare decisis carrie[d] enhanced force” because the Court was tasked
with “interpret[ing] a statute.”  Id. at 456.  For “a constitutional case” like Williams, “critics of [the Court’s]
ruling” cannot “take their objections across the street”
where “Congress can correct any mistake it sees.”  Id.
Unless the Court fixes its errant decision in Williams,
defendants like Mr. Kian have no recourse.
Kimble’s observation that stare decisis i s  a t  i t s
“acme” in cases involving “property and contract rights”
is likewise inapposite.  Fla.Br.36 (quoting 576 U.S.  at
457).  A constitutional right cannot be reduced to room
sizes or contracts for court services.  Fla.Br.36-37.  This
case instead involves a fundamental criminal procedure
protection, where “stare decisis is at its nadir.”  Alleyne
v. United States, 570 U.S. 99, 116 n.5 (2013).  Florida’s
own authority draws this distinction between “property” rights and “procedural … rules.”  Payne v. Tennessee, 501 U.S. 808, 828 (1991), cited in Fla.Br.33.  And
it could not be otherwise—constitutional protections will
almost always require more process, which in turn requires space and resources to provide that process.

15


Nor would preserving Williams “promote[] the evenhanded, predictable, and consistent” development of
the law.  Fla.Br.33.  “[ S]tare decisis does not prevent
[this Court] from overruling a previous decision where
there has been a significant change in, or subsequent development of, our constitutional law.”  Agostini v. Felton, 521 U.S. 203, 235-236 (1997).  Ramos was that kind
of significant change; it fundamentally disagreed with
Williams by requiring “trial by an impartial jury” to be
defined by reference to its “original public meaning,” not
its “function.”  Ramos, 590 U.S. at 89, 91-92, 94.
B. Williams Rejected The Original Public Meaning Of “Trial By An Impartial Jury”
Florida next reimagines Williams as an originalist
decision that “carefully examin[ed] text and history,” as
well as “the ‘common law’ practice of empaneling 12 jurors.”  Fla.Br.i, 34.  In reality, Williams’s limited historical analysis indicated “the jury at common law was composed of precisely 12.”  399 U.S. at 102.  It acknowledged
that “the usual expectation” at the Founding “may well”
have been “that the jury would consist of 12.”  Id. at 98.
Despite reaching these historical conclusions, the Court
stated that it could “not pretend to be able to divine precisely what the word ‘jury’ imported to the Framers, the
First Congress, or the States in 1789,” id. , unless there
was evidence “of an explicit decision to equate the constitutional and common-law characteristics of the jury,”
id. at 98-99.
Ramos rejected that mode of analysis.  It did not require proof of an explicit decision to codify each commonlaw feature; the Court recognized that the phrase “trial
by an impartial jury” “carried with it some meaning
about the content and requirements of a jury trial,” and
then asked what that meaning was based on

16


contemporaneous historical sour ces.  590 U.S. at 89-90.
The type of history Williams ultimately treated as beside the point, Ramos correctly held to be dispositive.
And Williams’s actual holding, Florida must concede,
relied on “the function that the particular feature performs and its relation to the purposes of the jury trial.”
399 U.S. at 99-100.
Florida’s assertion (Fla.Br.2) that Williams “differs
starkly” from Apodaca is groundless.  For example,
while Florida repeatedly implies (Fla.Br.2, 32, 49) that
Apodaca lacked precedential value, only a sliver of the
Ramos Court treated it as anything less than binding
precedent.  590 U.S. at 144-146 (Alito, J., dissenting).
More to the point, Apodaca described Williams as
having “consider[ed] a relate d issue” and followed the
earlier decision step by step.  406 U.S. at 406; see
Pet.Br.26.  As in Williams, the Court conceded the history:  “Like the requirement that juries consist of 12
men, the requirement of unanimity arose during the
Middle Ages[] and had become an accepted feature of the
common-law jury by the 18th century.”  Apodaca, 406
U.S. at 407-408.  Like Williams, it relied on supposed
ambiguity about the Framers’ “intent” to reject that history and “focus upon the function served by the jury in
contemporary society.”  Id. at 410.  And like Williams, it
concluded that the common-law requirement at issue
was unnecessary to serve that function.  Id. at 410-411.
Florida’s defense of Williams—that it reviewed the history before turning to function, Fla.Br.34—describes
Apodaca equally well.  Apodaca employed the “same

17


fundamental mode of analysis as that in Williams[.]”
Ramos, 590 U.S. at 157 (Alito, J., dissenting).4
C. Williams’s Functionalist Reasoning Is Wrong
Even On Its Own Terms
Florida’s claim (Fla.Br.22-24, 41-44) that a six-member jury can serve the same function as a 12-member
jury has already been effectively rejected by this Court.
See Ballew v. Georgia, 435 U.S. 223, 232-233 (1978).  Sixperson juries are less representative, less consistent,
and more likely to rule against a criminal defendant.
Pet.Br.30-34.
Florida faults Mr. Kian for not citing studies showing six-person verdicts are “less reliable or accurate.”
Fla.Br.43.  But Ballew did precisely that, explaining that
“post-Williams studies … raise significant doubts about
the consistency and reliability of the decisions of smaller
juries,” including because they show a decline in jury
size “leads to inaccurate fact-finding” and makes it more
difficult “to obtain an accurate result.”  435 U.S. at 232-
233, 235.
Florida’s studies (Fla.Br.43) do not rebut Ballew’s
conclusions.  One article did not analyze six-person juries
at all, and instead considered whether breaking a 12-
member jury into four-person discussion groups would
promote more effective deliberation.  Waller et al.,
Twelve (Not So) Angry Men, 14 Grp. Processes & Intergrp. Rels. 835, 839 (2011).  The others either studied

4 Florida also contends that “changes in ‘interpretive methodology’ do not render all precedents employing the old methodology
bad law.”  Fla.Br.34.  But Williams applied the wrong interpretive
method to the same constitutional term in the same amendment at
issue in Ramos.  The Court should not permit that term to retain “a
split personality.”  United States v. Davis, 588 U.S. 445, 456 (2019).

18


(1) unconstitutional five-member groups, Fay et al.,
Group Discussion as Interact ive Dialogue or as Serial
Monologue, 11 Psychol. Sci. 481, 481 (2000), or (2) mathematical models, Mukhopadhaya, Jury Size and the Free
Rider Problem, 19 J.L. Econ. & Org. 24, 27-43 (2003);
Luppi & Parisi, Jury Size and the Hung-Jury Paradox,
42 J. Legal Stud. 399, 407-416 (2013); Guerra et al., Accuracy of Verdicts , 28 Sup. Ct. Econ. Rev. 221, 225-232
(2020).  And the lone study Florida cites to support its
claim (Fla.Br.43) that “smaller juries, deciding unanimously, are just as accurate as 12-person juries” relies
on an inapposite comparison—large nonunanimous juries versus small unanimous juries—and expressly assumes no deliberation.  Guerra, at 228 n.17, 232.
Florida’s assertions (Fla.Br.41-42) about conviction
rates are similarly weak.  Florida contends that six-person juries protect criminal defendants because Florida’s
2022-2024 felony conviction rate was lower than Texas’s,
California’s, and New York’s.  Id.  But Florida’s amici
admit that “[b]ecause units of  analysis, trial modes, and
selection into trial differ across [such] systems, the
cross-state comparisons” are at best “descriptive evidence,” and “do not show causation.”  America.First.Br.10.  That makes sense:  In Florida, noncapital felonies can be charged by information— i.e., a decision made solely in the prosecutor’s discretion.  Fla. R.
Crim. P. 3.140(a)(2), (g).  Texas and New York generally
require grand jury indictments, Tex. Const. art.I, §10;
N.Y. Const. art.I, §6, and California requires preliminary hearings before a magistrate, Cal. Penal Code
§859b; Cal. Const. art.I, §14.  Given that Florida provides
no such process at the outset of a criminal prosecution, it

19


is little surprise that Florida’s ultimate conviction rate is
lower.5
Finally, while Florida (Fla.Br.44 n.24) criticizes
drawing a distinction between “six rather than 12 jurors” as founded on a “hunch,” its own legislature drew
that line—requiring 12-person juries for the cases with
the highest stakes (capital cases) and six-person juries
for the rest, see Fla.Br.4.  Other States that permit small
juries for felony offenses draw a similar distinction,
guaranteeing 12-person juries for at least capital cases.
See, e.g., Ariz. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 21-102; La. Code Crim.
Proc. Ann. art.782; Conn. Gen. Stat. Ann. §54-82(c); Ind.
Code Ann. §35-37-1-1(b); Utah Code Ann. §78B-1-
104(1)(a).
D. Williams Has Caused Negative Consequences
Florida dismisses Williams’s negative jurisprudential and real-world consequences without addressing the
bulk of Mr. Kian’s arguments.  E.g., Fla.Br.40-41.  “Perhaps concluding that silence is the better part of advocacy,” Fla.Br.24-25, Florida ignores entirely, for example, that Ballew struggled to apply Williams’s functionalist approach and admitted the weakness of Williams’s
empirical claims.  Supra p.17.
Florida is also demonstrably wrong when it suggests (Fla.Br.50-51) that no States adopted a smaller
jury size as a method “of disenfranchising black jurors.”

seem in some instances to be co mparing other States’ conviction
rates for felonies and misdemeanors against Florida’s rate of felony
convictions.  For example, while Florida asserts California’s conviction rate in 2024 was 81%, the so urce it cites indicates California
juries returned convictio ns in 72% of felony jury trials—less than
the rate reported for Florida.  Fla.Br.42 n.19.

20


In fact, “[d]uring the Jim Crow era, some States restricted the size of juries … as part of a deliberate and
systematic effort to suppress minority voices in public
affairs.”  Khorrami, 143 S.Ct. at 27 (Gorsuch, J., dissenting from denial of certiorari).  South Carolina expressly
targeted Black defendants.  Supra p.12.  And Louisiana
constitutionalized smaller juries at a convention meant
to “establish the supremacy of the white race,” Ramos,
590 U.S. at 87 & n.1; La. Const. art.116 (1898).  Louisiana’s prosecutors respond that the State first authorized
smaller juries in its 1879 constitution, and the 1898 convention merely “further codified this practice.”  Louisiana DA Br.9-11.  At best, this moves the racist origin of
smaller juries to two years after federal troops withdrew from Louisiana.  UVA, Miller Center of Public Affairs, Rutherford B. Hayes—Key Events , https://tinyurl.com/mtx7ee7w.
Florida itself has a more complex history, but it still
indicates racist origins.  Pet.Br.11-12.  Florida primarily
argues the constitutional amendment allowing the State
to reduce jury size received support from Black legislators.  Fla.Br.50.  But all 14 participating Black legislators
voted against the statute that actually reduced the size
of noncapital juries.  1877 House Journal 187-188; 1877
Senate Journal 208; Brown Jr., Florida’s Black Public
Officials, 1867-1924, at 145-148 (1998) (listing legislators).  And in the same session, the legislature enacted
(or reaffirmed) a host of racist measures to reduce Black
participation in public life, including a juror qualifications statute and convict-leasing statutes under which
Black Floridians were “aggressively arrested and imprisoned under expanded criminal codes” and leased out
to “private plantations and factories.”  NAACP.Br.29;
Pet.Br.12.  Florida claims its six-person juries were a
cost-saving measure, but the cited messages never

21


addressed jury size.  Fla.Br.50.  Instead, one asked to
cap juror pay, 1874 Senate Journal 16, and the second
called only for unspecified “reform,” 1877 Senate Journal
42-43.
E. The Asserted Reliance Interests Are Speculative And, Regardless, Outweighed By The
Importance Of The Jury Trial Right
Florida mostly relies on the same interest rejected
in Ramos: the need to retry a discrete number of nonfinal convictions.  But because almost any new rule of
criminal procedure will “affect[] significant numbers of
pending cases across the whole country,” Ramos, 590
U.S. at 108, Florida pads its estimate by sweeping in
many cases not at issue here—misdemeanors, federal
criminal jury trials, and federal civil jury trials.
First, Florida speculates that “more than half of the
states … would be required to retry (or dismiss) many,
many criminal cases.”  Fla.Br.35.  But it does not dispute
that only seven States use small juries in felony cases.
And this case concerns Mr. Kian’s felony convictions.
Supra pp.2-3.  The Court thus need not resolve anything
about misdemeanors or what constitutes a serious crime.
Fla.Br.35-36; U.S.Br.16-17.  Regardless, Florida’s assertion (Fla.Br.36) that there are millions of misdemeanors
filed nationwide each year says nothing about how many
of those cases involved “serious” misdemeanors, went to
a small jury, ended in a conviction, and remain on direct
review.
Second, Florida suggests this Court’s ruling will impact federal verdicts.  Fla.Br.37-38.  But as the U.S.
acknowledges, “federal criminal juries generally consist
of 12 people,” and Mr. Kian has not “challenge[d] the independent constitutionality of Federal Rule” 23(b)(3)’s

22


narrow exception to that principle.  U.S.Br.1, 6; see also
U.S.Br.29 (“Rule 23(b)(3) is meaningfully different from
laws like Florida’s”).  Tellingly, moreover, neither Florida nor the U.S. identify how many 11-person jury trial
convictions are actually pending on direct appeal.
Third, this case says nothing about the scope of the
Seventh Amendment.  The Seventh Amendment’s reference to “Suits at common law”—which “is not directed
to jury characteristics, such as size, but rather defines
the kind of cases for which jury trial is preserved,” Colgrove v. Battin, 413 U.S. 149, 152 (1973)—could well preclude adopting attributes of the jury in that context.
There is also good reason for the Sixth Amendment to
be more protective than the Seventh, as it protects “human liberty” rather than “property.”  Stogner v. California, 539 U.S. 607, 632 (2003).  Finally, as Florida’s own
examples show, the history of 12-person juries in civil
cases is decidedly more mixed than the history in criminal cases.  See supra pp.7, 9-10.
Fourth, Florida and its amici overstate the practical
difficulties of adopting 12-person juries.  For example,
Florida asserts its courthouses cannot fit six more
chairs.  Fla.Br.37.  But Florida already seats 12-person
juries in every capital trial, and its noncapital jury boxes
routinely hold more than six jurors because Florida
seats alternates.  Fla.Crim.Def.Lawyers.Br.24-25 (citing
Fla. R. Crim. P. 3.280).  Florida’s clerks predict higher
jury-management costs associated with larger juries,
supposedly leading to longer, more expensive, and
more administratively burde nsome criminal trials.
Fla.Clerks.Br.14-19.  But all States already empanel
12-person juries in at least some cases involving serious
crimes without the consequences Florida and its

23


amici predict.  Utah.Crim.Def.Lawyers.Br.20-21; National.Crim.Def.Lawyers.Br.17.
While Florida claims “[m]any” of the 5,200 pending
criminal direct appeals in Florida would be affected,
Fla.Br.i, 32, 35, it cites no source for this number—and
thus makes it impossible to determine how many of
those cases involved felonies or whether the defendant
preserved a challenge to jury size.  Even the Floridaspecific statistics proffered by the U.S. are significantly
lower (1,413 jury-trial convi ctions in 2024-2025) and do
not appear to account for the fact that capital offenses
would have been heard by 12-person juries.  See
U.S.Br.22.
Florida is left with the same fearmongering about
other criminal procedure decisions raised in Ramos.
Fla.Br.44-49.  None of those decisions involves the Sixth
Amendment’s right to a jury trial.  And unlike Williams,
Florida has not shown that those cases employ the “same
fundamental mode of analysis” as Apodaca.  Ramos, 590
U.S. at 157 (Alito, J., dissent ing).  This case is thus
uniquely tied to the Court’s decision in Ramos.  This
Court need go no further than holding that because Apodaca fell, Williams must fall as well.
CONCLUSION
The judgment below should be reversed.
